sections.h2: What makes an Arizona deed valid, including a quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
An Arizona deed has to be in writing, signed by the person giving up the property, delivered, and acknowledged before an authorized officer. A.R.S. 33-401 sets those rules for any conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold, or a term of more than one year. A quitclaim deed is held to the same basic standard as any other deed.

Signing is not enough on its own. Subsection B requires the grantor's signature and a proper acknowledgment, which is the notary step that lets the recorder accept the paper. If the acknowledgment has a flaw, the statute says a recorded deed is treated as properly acknowledged from the date it was recorded. That protects a deed after the fact, but you should not plan around it. Get the notary block right the first time.

One extra rule applies to certain regulated grantees such as entities under titles 6, 10 or 29. Their full name, address and state of organization must appear in the deed, though the statute says a failure to include them does not make the deed invalid.

sections.h2: Does an Arizona quitclaim deed need an affidavit of property value?
sections.html:
Usually a deed needs one, but a quitclaim deed made for no money is exempt. A.R.S. 11-1133 says each deed that transfers title must have a joint affidavit of the buyer and seller attached at recording, and the county recorder must refuse any deed without a complete affidavit unless it carries a notation of an exemption.

The affidavit asks for plain facts about the sale:

  • Names, mailing addresses and phone numbers for buyer and seller.
  • The address for the tax statement, the legal description and the situs address.
  • The sale date, the total consideration and the down payment, and how the deal was financed.
  • Whether personal property worth five percent or more of the price was included.
  • The assessor's parcel number and the relationship between the parties.
  • Whether a house will be owner-occupied or rented.

An affidavit counts as complete when every item is answered or marked "not applicable."

sections.h2: Which Arizona quitclaim transfers are exempt from the affidavit and fee?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed to quiet title or one executed for no monetary consideration is exempt, along with a short list of other transfers. The full list is in A.R.S. 11-1134. A few that come up for homeowners:

TransferStatute reference
Quitclaim to quiet title, or any quitclaim for no monetary consideration11-1134(A)(4)
Deed of gift11-1134(A)(7)
Conveyance made under a court order11-1134(A)(5)
Deed that confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed11-1134(B)(2)
Nominal-consideration residential transfer between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, or siblings11-1134(B)(3)
Transfer from a person to a trustee or from a trustee to a beneficiary, nominal consideration11-1134(B)(8)
Spouses to themselves to create community property with right of survivorship11-1134(B)(10)
Legal name change11-1134(B)(14)

The statute also requires that the exemption you claim be written on the face of the instrument at the time of recording. A deed that is exempt but does not say so can be refused like any other deed missing its affidavit.

sections.h2: What does a recorder look for on the quitclaim deed itself?
sections.html:
The recorder checks the form of the paper before anything else. A.R.S. 11-480 lists the conditions, and an instrument that fails one of them may be rejected when it is presented.

  • A caption that briefly states the nature of the document, such as "quitclaim deed."
  • An original that is legible enough to copy.
  • Original signatures, unless the law says otherwise.
  • For documents dated and executed on or after January 1, 1991, no wider than eight and one-half inches, no longer than fourteen inches, and type no smaller than ten point.

There is also a two-inch top margin on the first page for the recorder's stamp. The left three and one-half inches of that margin can show who asked for recording and where to return the document. If the first page does not comply, you attach a separate cover sheet that meets the requirement and shows the document's title. A half-inch margin applies on all sides, though failing it affects notice and is not a reason for rejection.

sections.h2: How much does the county recorder charge to record a quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
The standard county recorder fee in Arizona is $30 per instrument when no other fee is specified. A.R.S. 11-475 sets that figure, plus $15 per instrument for papers recorded at the request of the United States, the state or a political subdivision.

Certified copies cost $1 for each page or partial page, with $3 added for the recorder's certificate and seal. Check the recorder's own fee page for the county where the property sits before you send a check, since that office handles the filing.

Remember that the affidavit exemption in 11-1134 refers to "the affidavit and fee required by this article." The recorder's own fee in 11-475 is a different statute, so ask the recorder whether an exempt deed still pays the standard recording fee.

sections.h2: When does a quitclaim deed make sense if you plan to sell?
sections.html:
It makes sense when the goal is to fix or move title between people who already agree, such as removing a name after a divorce, adding a spouse, or moving a house into a family trust. It does not replace the sale paperwork when an outside buyer is paying for the house.

Think through these questions before you sign:

  • Who needs to be on title at closing? Ask the title company who must sign the sale deed.
  • Does a mortgage or tax balance remain? A deed between family members does not remove either one.
  • Is any money changing hands? Real consideration moves the transfer out of the no-money exemption and brings the affidavit back.
  • Will a title company insure the sale after the transfer? Ask before you record anything.

If a quitclaim is part of getting a house ready to sell, tell us what the situation is. We buy houses as-is across Arizona and the title company tells us what has to be cleared before closing.

sections.h2: What did we leave out of this Arizona quitclaim guide?
sections.html: We did not confirm each county recorder's online filing rules, notary rules beyond A.R.S. 33-401, or the effect of a quitclaim on title insurance and loans. Those answers depend on the recorder, the lender and the title insurer. A short call to the recorder in the county where the house sits answers most form questions in minutes.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed exempt from the Arizona affidavit of property value?
faqs.a: Yes, when it is a quitclaim to quiet title or is executed for no monetary consideration. A.R.S. 11-1134(A)(4) lists that exemption, and the exemption has to be written on the face of the deed at recording.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Arizona?
faqs.a: $30 per instrument is the standard county recorder fee under A.R.S. 11-475. Government-requested recordings are $15, and certified copies cost $1 per page plus $3 for the seal.

faqs.q: Does an Arizona deed need to be notarized?
faqs.a: Yes. A.R.S. 33-401 requires the grantor to sign and acknowledge the deed before an authorized officer. If the acknowledgment has a defect, a recorded deed is treated as properly acknowledged from the date of recording.

faqs.q: What size must an Arizona deed be?
faqs.a: No wider than 8.5 inches and no longer than 14 inches, with type no smaller than ten point, for documents executed on or after January 1, 1991. The first page needs a two-inch top margin for the recorder.

faqs.q: Can a quitclaim deed fix a mistake in an earlier deed?
faqs.a: A deed that confirms or corrects a previously recorded deed is exempt from the affidavit and fee under A.R.S. 11-1134(B)(2). Whether a quitclaim is the right tool for a given error is a question for a title company or attorney.
